items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small white insects are whiteflies that are feeding on your tomato leaves. First shake each tomato plant and look under the leaves to see how many insects are present. Then turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Set up yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies. For the approved spray and its rate, see ICAT.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is showing signs of a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service today so they can identify which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in shade, provide clean water nearby and avoid making him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you see on every animal in the herd, not only on the bull. Do not reuse the same injection needle on more than one animal because gall sickness can be transmitted that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy. The pattern you describe - even yellowing on the lower, older leaves while the top remains greenish, and short stature on worn soil - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant, and the merchant's package is for a soil that has lost organic matter, not what is left. What to do instead: rebuild the soil organic content with manure, compost, or unburnt residues. Then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. After these steps, request a soil check from ICAT and get the dose right for your plot.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you what is in it and I will not confirm it with a capful. A drum of unknown contents has no label and no dose, so any amount I suggested would be guesswork on your crop, and the cabbages could be damaged in ways you cannot see. What I can do is tell you to be wary of that offer and to ask ICAT which product and what it is actually contains, because a drum with no label is not handling a product at all. If you have to act, take the capful to them with a sign that says where the label should be, and wait until they have seen it before you move.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where you are, so here are both and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener, early in the season on old Kara land - matches nitrogen hunger, not a disease. No fungicide can green a hungry plant, and a big bag of compound fertilizer on a run-down soil rarely pays off. The correct step is to restore organic matter first: manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt. Then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. After these steps, ask ICAT for a soil check and the dose for your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: You should give an anticoccidial treatment in the feed or in the water right after you have removed the source of infection. First dry the litter immediately and replace it with fresh, dry bedding. Keep the house clean to prevent further buildup. Give an anticoccidial dose that is listed for the problem you are seeing. Separate the sick chicks from the healthy ones and provide them with clean water. Do not overcrowd the birds; give each chick enough space to move. If the chicks keep dying despite dry litter and treatment, see a veterinary auxiliary.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and I would rather say that than guess at the same time as you look. I can tell you what the signs are, and you have to see them. Shortage of feed on a pale dry colour is a sign of hunger in a hungry animal, not something that comes with a leaf, and a fungus on a leaf is a different thing entirely, so the leaf alone does not tell me whether it is hunger or a disease. What to do instead: separate the animal from the others where possible; give it water; look at the gums and the coat; note when this started and whether it started on some animals or all; take it to the veterinary service with those four points.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I am a model that runs in my head, without a camera, a microphone or any network. I fetch what I was trained on from these weights and answer textually, without moving a physical part of the machine. The cost is real: I cannot see images or hear voices, so I cannot help with a description of a crop or of a animal. I can still tell you which of the five common agricultural problems this is, and I will tell you why. Tell me what you saw on the field, and I will tell you what to do.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that runs in the moment and produces a flag. I answer as I read. There is one thing worth noting about my behaviour: when asked about a condition I was not taught, I tell you that rather than guessing something about it, and I point you to the service that can look at the plant or the animal. That is an honest admission of what I could not do, and it is the only way to keep a false answer from coming out. The cost of that is that I stop answering instead of producing a flagged answer.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: The two pests you describe are aphids and whiteflies, and they are not the same insect. First, look under the leaves of your tomato plants: a cloud of tiny white insects that flies up and settles back down means whiteflies are present. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants to be sure. If you find many whiteflies, pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds around the plot. If aphids are dominant, use a strong jet of water on the plants and rely on ladybirds and lacewings that naturally eat them. For any pesticide, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from the LFM2-700M base model by agritgllm. The LFM2-700M was adapted from LFM2, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License, and quantized to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes. My specific size is determined during inference: about 740 million parameters, compared to the full 1.5 billion. The practical limitation is where the name "agritgllm" comes from, not the model's architecture. I run in llama.cpp on a CPU alone, with no GPU or network call.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and they add up quickly. I cannot know today's weather or tomorrow's, so I will not tell you what the rains are likely to be. I cannot look at a photograph. I cannot give you a dose that is not written in the material I was taught, and a wrong dose is not just a guess I made; it is someone who has read me and forgot to check it. The last one is the one that should scare you: outside Togolese agriculture I am very bad at things that do not come out of training, and that is why I say no.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, a specialized version of the LFM2-700M model crafted by team agritgllm for the purpose of assisting Togolese farmers with agricultural matters. In contrast to the general-purpose LFM2-700M model, AgriTG LLM has been specifically adapted through fine-tuning to address the unique challenges and contexts of Togolese agriculture. This targeted adaptation allows AgriTgllm to deliver more precise and relevant advice in areas such as local crop management, livestock care, seasonal weather predictions, and market price insights, all while operating offline on a laptop without requiring internet access.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. Three bags is more than the yield per bag would be, and it is the opposite of what I was taught: the brochure says 100 kg of NPK per hectare, so three bags is three times the amount of fertiliser per hectare, not three times the crop. What three bags does give you is the risk, because the brochure warns against buying a broad-spectrum NPK and a systemic fungicide on a guess: on run-down soil the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. The right answer depends on the soil, which you can get from ICAT.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Eight birds dead in one morning is far too many to ignore, and it points to something spreading faster than a flock that has been exposed to disease. First, isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Then burn or bury the dead birds together with the soiled litter and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the remaining birds with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the vaccination schedule. If you need help right away, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with spray. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean cuttings, ITRA can provide them. I cannot give you any other service details.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: I cannot name a disease from those symptoms. The long pale broken lines along the veins with stunted small leaves are typical of maize streak virus, which is carried by leafhoppers. Maize streak virus does not have any cure once infected, so you must rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. Avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. For the next season, ask ICAT for an improved MSV-tolerant variety. I cannot give you a specific product or dose.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate groundnut rosette and there is no cure once infected, so you must act to stop it spreading. Remove and destroy any severely affected plants right away. Keep the field completely weed-free because weeds serve as hosts for the aphid vectors. Sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing to obtain a dense stand that is less vulnerable. Rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants now to cut the source of the virus. For the following season, plant a tolerant groundnut variety. You can obtain resistant varieties from ICAT.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what tablet to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for AgriTG LLM, which is a tool for farming. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which crop it was for. Do not wait for signs, because delay can be the difference between a mild case and something serious. Afterwards, keep the sowing seed in a closed, marked container, out of reach of children and away from food, and wash your hands after handling it.
